evidence.description: The timer loop does not account for the time taken to execute the asynchronous calls (totalInvestedAt and getTimerInterval), causing the actual interval to be longer than intended.

candidates.explanation: The while loop uses Task.sleep for the duration of the interval but does not subtract the execution time of the asynchronous operations inside the loop. This causes the timer to 'drift' over time.
candidates.title: Drifting timer loop

evidence.description: The class uses a singleton pattern (shared) while also having an initializer that starts a side-effect (startTimer), which can lead to multiple timer instances if the initializer is called more than once.

candidates.explanation: Calling startTimer() inside init() is a side-effect. Combined with the public singleton, this can make the lifecycle of the timer task difficult to manage and reason about.
candidates.title: Side-effect in initializer

evidence.description: The class conforms to Publisher but manages an internal array of subscriptions, which is not the standard way to implement a custom Publisher and may lead to incorrect behavior regarding subscription lifecycle.

candidates.explanation: The class manually maintains a list of subscriptions. In Swift's Combine framework, publishers typically manage their own demand and subscription lifecycle; manual tracking in a property like 'subscriptions' can lead to memory leaks or missed emissions.
candidates.title: Manual subscription management
